videos.title: Epictetus's Rule: Master Your Emotions in 45 Seconds
videos.script_preview: Every time you explode over disrespect, traffic, or delay, you surrender your freedom to external noise. Epictetus was born into slavery in Hierapolis before earning freedom and founding a Stoic school in Nicopolis. He taught that external events are entirely beyond your control, but your internal volition—prohairesis—is yours alone. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes his philosophy centers on self-management and the correct use of impressions. videos.topic: Memento Mori: Why Remembering Death Makes You Fearless
videos.title: Memento Mori: Why Remembering Death Makes You Fearless
videos.script_preview: You waste whole years agonizing over social anxiety and trivial failures, acting as if your time on Earth is infinite. The Romans built a ruthless mental filter around Memento Mori—Latin for 'remember that you must die.' Derived from the future imperative meminī and infinitive morī, it is not a gentle thought, but an urgent command. The ancient philosopher Democritus locked himself inside secluded stone tombs, using proximity to death to eliminate fear. videos.topic: How to Stop Being Lazy: The Brutal Stoic Discipline Formula
videos.title: The Brutal Stoic Formula to End Laziness
videos.script_preview: You are not suffering from burnout. You are actively coddling your own laziness. In 170 AD, Emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote notes to himself while fighting brutal winter campaigns at the Granova River. Documented as Ta eis heauton, these private Greek journals were never meant for publication—only self-mastery. His core Stoic doctrine: virtue alone is good, while external comfort is completely indifferent to happiness. videos.topic: The Power of Moving in Silence: Why Stoics Never Speak
videos.title: The Power of Moving in Silence: Why Stoics Never Speak
videos.script_preview: Your mouth is the leak in your ambition. Every time you announce your plans, your brain triggers a false sense of accomplishment—dopamine for talk, not work. You are trading reality for the cheap validation of others. Marcus Aurelius warned: 'Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.' Stoic logic isn't about public performance; it is the mind in rational dialogue with itself, not a desperate plea for attention. Weak men need an audience to confirm their existence. videos.topic: Seneca's Guide to Overcoming Anxiety and Fear
videos.title: Seneca’s Brutal Rule for Ending Anxiety
videos.script_preview: Your anxiety is not a reaction to your environment; it is a failure of your foresight. You are suffering because you refuse to accept the volatility of existence. Seneca, a man who navigated the treacherous court of Nero, taught a cold, tactical truth: 'We suffer more in imagination than in reality.' The weak man blinds himself, hoping for safety, and is shattered when his fragile world collapses. The master does the opposite. He practices 'premeditatio malorum.'
